title: Lifting primitive roots to prime powers
question: When does a generator modulo \(p\) remain a generator modulo \(p^2\)?
summary: A primitive root modulo an odd prime lifts to maximal order at every higher prime power if its first lift is not exceptional. The exact test is whether \(a^{p-1}\not\equiv1\pmod{p^2}\). If a chosen representative fails, adding \(p\) changes the next digit and repairs the test.
definition: For a prime \(p\) and a nonzero integer \(M\), let \(v_p(M)\) be the largest nonnegative integer \(r\) for which \(p^r\mid M\). A representative \(a\) of a primitive root modulo an odd prime \(p\) is called exceptional at the first lift when \(a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{p^2}\).

A primitive root modulo \(p^k\) is a unit of order \(\varphi(p^k)=(p-1)p^{k-1}\). The order is computed for the chosen residue class; changing an integer representative by a multiple of \(p\) can change its class modulo \(p^2\).
theorem: Let \(p\) be an odd prime and let \(a\) be an integer whose class has order \(p-1\) modulo \(p\). If \(a^{p-1}\not\equiv1\pmod{p^2}\), then \(\operatorname{ord}_{p^k}(a)=(p-1)p^{k-1}\) for every \(k\ge1\). If the chosen representative is exceptional, then \(a+p\) is still a primitive root modulo \(p\) and is nonexceptional modulo \(p^2\). Consequently, every primitive root class modulo \(p\) has a representative that lifts to primitive roots at all powers \(p^k\).
proof: We first establish a divisibility fact. Suppose \(p\) is odd and \(u=1+c p^r\), where \(r\ge1\) and \(p\nmid c\). The binomial expansion gives \(u^p-1=c p^{r+1}+\sum_{i=2}^{p-1}\binom pi c^i p^{ri}+c^p p^{rp}\). For \(2\le i\le p-1\), the binomial coefficient is divisible by \(p\), so that term is divisible by \(p^{1+2r}\), hence by \(p^{r+2}\). The last term is also divisible by \(p^{r+2}\), since \(rp\ge r+2\) for odd \(p\) and \(r\ge1\). Therefore \(u^p-1\equiv c p^{r+1}\pmod{p^{r+2}}\), and \(v_p(u^p-1)=r+1\).

If \(s\ge1\) and \(p
mid s\), then \(u^s-1=(u-1)(1+u+\cdots+u^{s-1})\). The second factor is congruent to \(s
ot\equiv0\pmod p\), so \(v_p(u^s-1)=v_p(u-1)\). Writing any positive integer \(t\) as \(p^j s\) with \(p
mid s\) and iterating the two facts proves \(v_p(u^t-1)=v_p(u-1)+v_p(t)\).

Now put \(u=a^{p-1}\). The primitive-root hypothesis gives \(u\equiv1\pmod p\), while the nonexceptional condition gives \(v_p(u-1)=1\). If \(a^m\equiv1\pmod{p^k}\), reduction modulo \(p\) and \(\operatorname{ord}_p(a)=p-1\) imply \(p-1\mid m\). Write \(m=(p-1)t\). The divisibility fact gives \(p^k\mid a^m-1\) exactly when \(1+v_p(t)\ge k\), or equivalently \(p^{k-1}\mid t\). Conversely, taking \(t=p^{k-1}\) makes \(p^k\mid a^{(p-1)t}-1\). Hence the positive exponents returning \(a\) to \(1\) modulo \(p^k\) are exactly the multiples of \((p-1)p^{k-1}\); the least such exponent is the order claimed. This includes \(k=1\).

Finally, suppose the representative \(a\) is exceptional. The binomial theorem modulo \(p^2\) gives \( (a+p)^{p-1}\equiv a^{p-1}+(p-1)a^{p-2}p\pmod{p^2}\). Since \(a^{p-1}\equiv1\pmod{p^2}\), this is \(1-a^{p-2}p\pmod{p^2}\). Because \(p\nmid a\), the coefficient \(a^{p-2}\) is nonzero modulo \(p\), so this is not congruent to \(1\pmod{p^2}\). The integer \(a+p\) has the same residue as \(a\) modulo \(p\), so it remains a primitive root there and satisfies the nonexceptional condition.

example.prompt: Compare two representatives of the primitive root \(2\) modulo \(5\), and repair the exceptional one.
steps: Modulo \(5\), the powers of \(2\) are \(2,4,3,1\), so its order is \(4\). For the representative \(2\), \(2^4=16\not\equiv1\pmod{25}\); it is nonexceptional. Also \(2^{10}=1024\equiv-1\pmod{25}\), so \(2^{20}\equiv1\pmod{25}\). Its order modulo \(25\) is a multiple of \(4\) by reduction modulo \(5\), divides \(20\) because \(2^{20}\equiv1\), and is not \(4\); hence it is \(20\).

The representative \(7=2+5\) has the same order \(4\) modulo \(5\), but \(7^4=2401\equiv1\pmod{25}\). Its order modulo \(25\) is therefore exactly \(4\): it divides \(4\) and its reduction modulo \(5\) has order \(4\).

Repair it by adding \(5\) again, obtaining \(12\). Now \(12^4=20736\equiv11\not\equiv1\pmod{25}\), while \(12^{20}=(12^4)^5\equiv11^5\equiv1\pmod{25}\). Its reduction has order \(4\), so the same divisor check gives order \(20\) modulo \(25\).
example.conclusion: The integer \(7\) is an exceptional representative even though its residue is primitive modulo \(5\); the repaired representative \(12\) has maximal order modulo \(25\).

practice.prompt: Use \(3\) to give an order certificate for a primitive root modulo \(49\).
hints: First list the powers of \(3\) modulo \(7\) to establish order \(6\).
Compute \(3^6-1\) and use the nonexceptional lifting result.
practice.answer: Modulo \(7\), the powers of \(3\) at exponents \(1\) through \(6\) are \(3,2,6,4,5,1\), so its order is \(6\). Also \(3^6-1=728=7\cdot104\), and \(7\nmid104\), so \(3^6\not\equiv1\pmod{49}\). The lifting theorem gives \(\operatorname{ord}_{49}(3)=42\). For a direct certificate, \(3^{42}=(1+7\cdot104)^7\equiv1\pmod{49}\), so the order divides \(42\); reduction modulo \(7\) shows it is a multiple of \(6\). The only divisors of \(42\) that are multiples of \(6\) are \(6\) and \(42\), and the noncongruence at exponent \(6\) rules out the first.

caution: A primitive root class modulo \(p\) does not make every integer representative primitive modulo \(p^2\). The maximal-order conclusion needs the nonexceptional congruence; the repair changes the representative by \(p\) and is valid because the target class is modulo \(p\).
bridge: The lift theorem gives generators for odd prime powers. CRT combines unit groups at coprime moduli, while elements of order two explain why most combinations cannot be cyclic.

title: Exactly which moduli have primitive roots?
question: Why do some unit groups have no generator at all?
summary: The unit group is cyclic exactly for moduli \(2\), \(4\), odd prime powers, and twice odd prime powers. CRT creates multiple independent elements of order two when distinct odd primes or an incompatible power of two appear; the listed cases have explicit generators.
definition: For an integer \(n\ge2\), write \(U(n)=(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z)^\times\) for the multiplicative group of invertible residue classes. A primitive root modulo \(n\) is a generator of \(U(n)\), so its order equals \(\varphi(n)\), the number of classes relatively prime to \(n\).
A self-inverse element is a class \(x\) satisfying \(x^2=1\). Apart from the identity, such an element has order exactly \(2\).
theorem: For an integer \(n\ge2\), the group \(U(n)\) is cyclic if and only if \(n=2\), \(n=4\), \(n=p^k\), or \(n=2p^k\), where \(p\) is an odd prime and \(k\ge1\). Equivalently, these and only these moduli admit primitive roots.
proof: First prove existence for the listed moduli. For \(n=2\), \(U(2)=\{1\}\) is cyclic of order \(1\). For \(n=4\), the class \(3\) has order \(2=\varphi(4)\). If \(n=p^k\) with odd prime \(p\), exactly \(p^{k-1}\) of the \(p^k\) residue classes are divisible by \(p\); the rest are units, so \(\varphi(p^k)=(p-1)p^{k-1}\). U03 supplies a class of that order. Finally, CRT identifies \(U(2p^k)\) with \(U(2)\times U(p^k)\). The first factor is trivial, so a generator of \(U(p^k)\) corresponds to a generator of \(U(2p^k)\).

For nonexistence, use the fact that a cyclic group has at most one element of order \(2\): if a cyclic group has order \(h\), an element \(g^r\) has square one only when \(h\mid2r\), which has at most two exponent classes modulo \(h\), one of which is the identity. Thus more than two distinct solutions of \(x^2=1\) rule out cyclicity.

Factor \(n=2^a\prod_{i=1}^{r}p_i^{k_i}\), where the \(p_i\) are distinct odd primes and \(a,r\ge0\). If \(r\ge2\), CRT lets us choose independently \(1\) or \(-1\) in two odd-prime-power coordinates and \(1\) in every other coordinate. These give four distinct roots of \(x^2=1\), three nonidentity, so \(U(n)\) is not cyclic.

If \(a\ge3\), the four classes \(1\), \(-1\), \(1+2^{a-1}\), and \(-1+2^{a-1}\) are distinct odd classes modulo \(2^a\). Their squares are all congruent to \(1\pmod{2^a}\), since \((1\pm2^{a-1})^2=1\pm2^a+2^{2a-2}\equiv1\pmod{2^a}\). If odd prime-power factors are present, CRT combines each of these with \(1\) in the other coordinates. In either case \(U(n)\) has at least four roots of \(x^2=1\), so it is not cyclic.

The only remaining case with \(a=2\) is either \(n=4\), already included, or at least one odd prime-power factor. In the latter case CRT supplies the four distinct sign choices \((1,1),(-1,1),(1,-1),(-1,-1)\) from \(U(4)\times U(p^k)\) (and identity coordinates for any other factors). Three are nonidentity roots of \(x^2=1\), so the group is not cyclic. The remaining cases have \(a=0\) or \(1\) and at most one odd prime factor; for \(n\ge2\) these are exactly the listed forms.

example.prompt: Compare \(U(8)\) and \(U(10)\). Which one has a primitive root?
steps: The four units modulo \(8\) are \(1,3,5,7\). Their squares are all congruent to \(1\pmod8\), so every element has order at most \(2\). The group has four elements but no element of order \(4\), hence it is not cyclic.
The units modulo \(10\) are \(1,3,7,9\). The powers \(3,9,7,1\) show that \(3\) has order \(4=\varphi(10)\), so it is a primitive root modulo \(10\).
example.conclusion: The power-of-two obstruction rules out a generator modulo \(8\), while \(10=2\cdot5\) is an allowed modulus and \(3\) generates its unit group.

practice.prompt: Classify which of \(8,9,12,14,16,18,25,30\) admit primitive roots, using the theorem before testing residues.
hints: Factor each modulus into a power of \(2\) and distinct odd prime powers.
Only one odd prime may occur, and the power of \(2\) may be at most \(2\) when an odd factor is present.
practice.answer: The allowed forms are \(9=3^2\), \(14=2\cdot7\), \(18=2\cdot3^2\), and \(25=5^2\); these admit primitive roots. The moduli \(8=2^3\) and \(16=2^4\) are excluded by the four self-inverse classes, \(12=4\cdot3\) is excluded by independent signs in \(U(4)\times U(3)\), and \(30=2\cdot3\cdot5\) is excluded by its two odd-prime factors.

caution: The additive group \(\mathbb Z/n\mathbb Z\) is cyclic for every positive \(n\); this theorem classifies the different group of units. The modulus must satisfy \(n\ge2\).
bridge: When a unit group is cyclic, choose one generator and assign each element its unique exponent modulo the group order. Power equations then become linear congruences.

title: Indices and power-congruence fibers
question: Why does \(x^k=a\) have either zero or a predictable number of solutions in a cyclic group?
summary: A generator assigns each group element a unique exponent modulo the group order. Under this coordinate system, taking a power is multiplication of exponents, so the linear-congruence theorem gives the exact existence condition and number of roots.
definition: Let \(G=\langle g\rangle\) be a cyclic unit group of order \(h\ge1\). Every \(a\in G\) has a unique index \(s\) modulo \(h\) such that \(a=g^s\); choose its canonical index with \(0\le s<h\).
For a positive integer \(k\), the power map sends \(x\) to \(x^k\). A fiber over \(a\) is the set of all \(x\in G\) with \(x^k=a\).
theorem: Let \(G=\langle g\rangle\) be cyclic of order \(h\), let \(a=g^s\), and let \(k\ge1\). Put \(d=\gcd(k,h)\). The equation \(x^k=a\) has a solution in \(G\) if and only if \(d\mid s\); when it is solvable it has exactly \(d\) solutions. Equivalently, in this cyclic group it is solvable if and only if \(a^{h/d}=1\).
proof: The map from exponent classes modulo \(h\) to \(G\), sending \(r\) to \(g^r\), is onto because \(g\) generates. It is one-to-one because \(g^r=g^t\) implies \(g^{r-t}=1\), and the order \(h\) means \(h\mid r-t\). Thus every possible root is uniquely \(x=g^r\) for an exponent class \(r\pmod h\).

The equation \(x^k=a\) is therefore equivalent to \(g^{kr}=g^s\), or \(kr\equiv s\pmod h\). If \(d=\gcd(k,h)\) does not divide \(s\), no such congruence can hold. If \(d\mid s\), divide by \(d\) to obtain \(k' r\equiv s'\pmod{h'}\), where \(k'=k/d\), \(h'=h/d\), and \(s'=s/d\). Since \(\gcd(k',h')=1\), Bézout’s identity gives an inverse for \(k'\) modulo \(h'\), so there is one solution class \(r_0\pmod{h'}\).

Viewed modulo \(h=d h'\), that class has exactly the \(d\) distinct representatives \(r_0+jh'\) for \(j=0,1,\ldots,d-1\). They all solve the original congruence, and every solution reduces to \(r_0\pmod{h'}\), so there are no others. The exponent-class bijection transfers these to exactly \(d\) roots in \(G\).

Finally, since \(a=g^s\), the condition \(a^{h/d}=1\) is equivalent to \(g^{s h/d}=1\), which by the order of \(g\) holds exactly when \(h\mid s h/d\), or \(d\mid s\). This criterion depends on \(G\) being cyclic with the stated generator and order.

The equal-fiber principle needs less structure. In any finite abelian group \(H\), the map \(T:H\to H\), \(T(x)=x^k\), is a homomorphism. If \(T(x_0)=a\), then \(T(x)=a\) exactly when \(T(xx_0^{-1})=1\), so the fiber above \(a\) is \(x_0\ker T\). Multiplication by \(x_0\) is a bijection from \(\ker T\) to that fiber. Thus every nonempty fiber has \(\lvert\ker T\rvert\) elements, whether or not \(H\) is cyclic.

example.prompt: Solve \(x^2\equiv2\pmod7\) using indices to the generator \(3\).
steps: The powers of \(3\) modulo \(7\) are \(3,2,6,4,5,1\), so \(3\) has order \(h=6\), and \(2\equiv3^2\pmod7\). The target index is \(s=2\).
Here \(d=\gcd(2,6)=2\), and \(2\mid s\), so there are exactly two solutions. Their exponent indices solve \(2r\equiv2\pmod6\), namely \(r\equiv1,4\pmod6\).
The corresponding residues are \(3^1\equiv3\pmod7\) and \(3^4\equiv4\pmod7\). Directly, \(3^2=9\equiv2\pmod7\) and \(4^2=16\equiv2\pmod7\).
example.conclusion: The two roots are \(3\) and \(4\), matching the fiber size \(d=2\).

practice.prompt: Compare the solutions of \(x^2=1\) in \(U(7)\) and \(U(8)\), and explain why the cyclic \(\gcd(k,h)\) formula applies to only one group.
hints: List the four units modulo \(8\) and square each.
practice.answer: In \(U(7)=\langle3\rangle\), the target \(1\) has index \(s=0\). With \(h=6\) and \(d=\gcd(2,6)=2\), the exponent equation \(2r\equiv0\pmod6\) gives \(r=0,3\), hence roots \(1\) and \(6\). In \(U(8)\), the units are \(1,3,5,7\), and each square is \(1\pmod8\), so the target \(1\) has four roots. The cyclic formula cannot be applied because \(U(8)\) is not cyclic; indeed, treating its size \(4\) as a cyclic order would incorrectly predict only \(\gcd(2,4)=2\) roots. Also \(3^2\equiv1\pmod8\), yet \(x^2\equiv3\pmod8\) has no solution, illustrating why the cyclic criterion \(a^{h/d}=1\) is not valid for \(U(8)\).

caution: Equal sizes of nonempty fibers do not require cyclicity: for any homomorphism of finite groups, each nonempty fiber is a coset of its kernel. Here the power map is a homomorphism because the unit group is abelian. The numerical formula \(\lvert\ker(x\mapsto x^k)\rvert=\gcd(k,h)\) and the exponent test \(a^{h/\gcd(k,h)}=1\) are the cyclic specializations; do not apply them to a noncyclic group without checking its structure.
bridge: Once a generator exists, exponent coordinates reduce every power equation to a linear congruence. When no generator exists, solutions must be analyzed through the actual group structure or by coprime local factors.
